outline: Superposition adds instantaneous displacements of waves of the same type at a point. Oppositely travelling progressive waves of the same frequency and similar amplitude can form a stationary wave. Nodes have zero amplitude; antinodes have maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes or antinodes are separated by $\lambda/2$; a node to its nearest antinode by $\lambda/4$. Reflected microwaves, strings and air columns reveal these positions.

misconceptions.statement: Amplitude rather than instantaneous displacement is added.
misconceptions.refutation: The resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements at that point and time.

misconceptions.statement: A node merely has zero displacement at one instant.
misconceptions.refutation: A node has zero amplitude, so its displacement is zero at all times.
misconceptions.contrast: zero amplitude versus a momentary zero

misconceptions.statement: Adjacent nodes are one wavelength apart.
misconceptions.refutation: Adjacent nodes or antinodes are half a wavelength apart.

misconceptions.statement: Overlapping waves must be in phase to make a stationary wave.
misconceptions.refutation: They must travel in opposite directions with the same frequency and similar amplitude; their relative phase varies with position.

items.stem:
Two progressive waves meet at a point.
Which condition must be met for superposition of the waves to occur?

options.B: The waves must be of the same type.
options.C: The waves must be travelling in opposite directions.
options.D: The waves must meet in phase.

items.explanation: Waves of the same type can superpose. Coherence is unnecessary for superposition itself.

items.stem:
The principle of superposition states that a certain quantity is added when two or more waves
meet at a point.
What is this quantity?
items.explanation: Instantaneous displacement is summed. Amplitude is a maximum, not the quantity added at each point.

items.stem:
Two waves of the same type overlap.
When does the principle of superposition apply?

options.B: only when the waves have the same amplitude
options.C: only when the waves have the same frequency
options.D: only when the waves travel in opposite directions

items.explanation: Any overlapping waves of the same type superpose. Equal amplitude is only relevant to perfectly deep stationary-wave nodes.

items.stem: What happens when two waves superpose at a point?
items.explanation: Displacements add algebraically at the point. Adding amplitudes would ignore the signs and instantaneous phases.

items.stem: Which statement concerning a stationary wave is correct?

options.A: All the particles between two adjacent nodes oscillate in phase.
options.B: The amplitude of the stationary wave is equal to the amplitude of one of the waves creating it.
options.C: The wavelength of the stationary wave is equal to the separation of two adjacent nodes.
options.D: There is no displacement of a particle at an antinode at any time.

items.explanation: Particles within adjacent nodes are in phase. B is wrong because antinode amplitude is the sum of contributing amplitudes.

items.stem:
Two progressive sound waves move in opposite directions and superpose to form a stationary
wave.
Which statement describes an antinode of this stationary wave?

options.A: a position where the phase difference between the two waves is always 0°
options.B: a position where the phase difference between the two waves is always 180°
options.C: a position where the stationary wave has maximum amplitude
options.D: a position where the stationary wave has minimum amplitude

items.explanation: An antinode has maximum stationary-wave amplitude. D instead describes a node.

items.stem:
Two progressive waves overlap.
What is an essential condition for the two waves to form a stationary wave?

options.C: The waves travel in opposite directions.
options.D: The waves travel in the same direction.

items.explanation: Opposite propagation directions are essential to form a stationary pattern. D gives travelling overlap instead.

flashcards.back: When two or more waves of the same type meet at a point, the resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements at that point.
A node is a position of zero amplitude. An antinode is a position of maximum amplitude.

flashcards.front: How are node and antinode separations related to wavelength?
flashcards.back: Adjacent nodes or antinodes: $\lambda/2$; nearest node to antinode: $\lambda/4$.

9702-8.1.1.motivate: When two pulses meet on a rope, what shape does the rope take at their overlap? The answer follows from adding what each pulse would do at the same point.
9702-8.1.1.establish: The principle of superposition states: when two or more waves of the same type meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the displacements of the individual waves at that point. Displacement is signed and instantaneous. For example, $+3$ mm and $-2$ mm combine to $+1$ mm. Amplitude is the maximum possible displacement of one wave and must not replace displacement in the statement. The principle applies whenever waves of the same type overlap; equal amplitude, coherence and opposite travel directions are not prerequisites for superposition itself.
9702-8.1.1.connect: Stationary waves are a special outcome of superposition: the opposing progressive waves repeatedly combine to produce a fixed pattern.
9702-8.1.1.note:
- Add instantaneous, signed displacements at the same point.
- Resultant displacement equals their algebraic sum.
- Equal amplitudes are not required for superposition.
9702-8.1.1.self_explain: Two pulses have displacements $+4$ mm and $-3$ mm at one point. Explain which quantities you add and why the resultant is positive.

9702-8.1.2.motivate: How could you observe a wave pattern that stays in place even though its component waves move? Use reflection to send a wave back through the incident wave.
9702-8.1.2.establish: For microwaves, aim a transmitter at a metal reflector and move a detector along the path. Alternating signal maxima and minima reveal the stationary pattern. For a stretched string, drive it at a suitable frequency while a reflected wave returns from the end; stable loops appear with nodes between them. For an air column, use a sound source and vary frequency or column length until resonance. The closed end is a displacement node and the open end a displacement antinode, assuming negligible end corrections. Powder in a horizontal tube gathers where air displacement amplitude is small, at nodes. These observations all arise from superposition of incident and reflected waves.
9702-8.1.2.connect: The fixed minima and maxima in each apparatus are the nodes and antinodes used to analyse formation and wavelength.
9702-8.1.2.note:
- Microwave: transmitter, reflector, moving detector.
- String: driver, reflected wave, stable loops.
- Air column: resonance; closed-end node, open-end antinode.
- Powder gathers at displacement nodes.
9702-8.1.2.self_explain: Describe one measurement or observation that shows a stationary wave in each of the three apparatuses.

9702-8.1.3.motivate: A snapshot of a string can cross equilibrium in many places. Which of those places stay still through an entire oscillation?
9702-8.1.3.establish: Two progressive waves of the same type and frequency, with similar amplitudes, travel in opposite directions and superpose. To construct the stationary wave graphically, draw both profiles on a common position axis and add their signed displacements point by point. Repeat at later instants. A node is a fixed point where the resultant amplitude is zero, so displacement is always zero. An antinode is a fixed point where the amplitude is maximum. At a particular instant even an antinode can have zero displacement, so one snapshot is insufficient to establish a node. All particles between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase; particles in neighbouring loops oscillate in antiphase.
9702-8.1.3.connect: The sequence of fixed nodes and antinodes supplies a spatial ruler for determining wavelength.
9702-8.1.3.note:
- Opposite directions, same frequency, similar amplitudes.
- Add two profiles point by point at successive times.
- Node: zero amplitude; antinode: maximum amplitude.
- Adjacent loops oscillate in antiphase.
9702-8.1.3.self_explain: How would two displacement snapshots distinguish a genuine node from a point momentarily at equilibrium?

9702-8.1.4.motivate: The wave moves back and forth, but the node positions stay fixed. Their spacing lets you measure the travelling waves' wavelength.
9702-8.1.4.establish: Adjacent nodes are separated by $\lambda/2$, as are adjacent antinodes. A node and its nearest antinode are separated by $\lambda/4$. Thus, if adjacent nodes or adjacent antinodes are a distance $d$ apart, $\lambda=2d$. To reduce measurement uncertainty, measure the distance between positions several intervals apart, divide by the number of intervals, then double. For example, the first to fifth node spans four intervals. In an air column the closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode; the shortest resonant closed-open column has $L=\lambda/4$ when end corrections are negligible. A fixed-fixed string's shortest pattern has $L=\lambda/2$.
9702-8.1.4.connect: Once wavelength is known, the progressive-wave relation $v=f\lambda$ can give frequency or speed when the other quantity is supplied.
9702-8.1.4.note:
- Adjacent nodes or antinodes: $\lambda/2$.
- Nearest node to antinode: $\lambda/4$.
- Count gaps, average their separation, then double.
- Closed-open fundamental: $L=\lambda/4$.
9702-8.1.4.self_explain: The first and fourth nodes are $0.90$ m apart. Explain the interval count before finding the wavelength.
